items.title: 4.7.1 Strategy for the identification of the limiting reactant

source_refs.note: Topic 4.7.1, printed pages 86-87, as printed: the three steps, the Did You Know box, and Sample Problems 4.17 and 4.18.

blocks.text: To identify a limiting reactant, the following three steps are performed.

items: Calculate the number of moles from the given amounts of reactants.
Find out the number of moles of product with the help of a balanced chemical equation.
Identify the reactant which produces the least amount of product as limiting reactant and the other as an excess reactant.

blocks.title: Did You Know?
blocks.text: Fire is a combustion reaction in which fuel and oxygen, O₂, combine, usually at high temperatures, to form water and carbon dioxide. Once the fire has started, it is self-supporting. An effective way to quench a fire is smothering, which reduces the amount of available oxygen below the level needed to support combustion. In other words, smothering decreases the amount of the excess reactant. Foams, inert gas, and CO₂ are effective substances for smothering.
Following numerical problem will make the idea clear.

blocks.title: Sample Problem 4.17 (Limiting Reactant)
blocks.problem: Calculate the mass of N₂ produced from 1.81 g of NH₃ (molar mass = 17.0 g mol⁻¹) and 90.4 g of CuO (molar mass = 79.5 g mol⁻¹) according to following balanced equation: 2NH₃(g) + 3CuO(s) → N₂(g) + 3Cu(s) + 3H₂O(g)
steps: Moles of NH₃ = 18.1 g of NH₃/ 17.0gmol⁻¹ = 1.06 mol
Moles of CuO = 90.4g of CuO/79.5gmol⁻¹ = 1.14 mol
Thus, CuO is the limiting reactant and the number of moles of N₂ produced will be 0.38 mol.
Hence, mass of N₂ produced = n x M = 0.38 mol x 17.0 g mol⁻¹

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question gives 1.81 g of NH₃ but the solution uses 18.1 g; the worked solution (1.06 mol NH₃, CuO limiting, 0.38 mol N₂) is consistent only with 18.1 g (with 1.81 g, NH₃ would be the limiting reactant). The mass of N₂ uses the molar mass of N₂, 28.0 g mol⁻¹, not 17.0 g mol⁻¹ (that of NH₃): 0.38 × 28.0 = 10.6 g, not 9.0 g.

blocks.title: Sample Problem 4.18 (Limiting Reactant)
blocks.problem: When aqueous solutions of Na₂SO₄ and Pb(NO₃)₂ are mixed, PbSO₄ precipitates down. Calculate the mass of PbSO₄ formed when 1.25 dm³ of 0.05 mol dm⁻³ Pb(NO₃)₂ and 2.00 dm³ of 0.025 mol dm⁻³ Na₂SO₄ are mixed. Na₂SO₄(aq) + Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) → PbSO₄(s) + NaNO₃(aq)
steps: The net ionic equation is Pb⁺²(aq) + SO₄⁻²(aq) → PbSO₄(s)
Since 0.05 mol dm⁻³ Pb(NO₃)₂ contains 0.05 mol dm⁻³ Pb²⁺ ions.
The formula : No. of moles = Concentration (mol dm⁻³ ) x Volume (dm³)
moles of Pb²⁺ ions = 0.05 mol dm⁻³ × 1.25 dm³ = 0.0625 mol
Thus, 0.025 mol dm⁻³ Na₂SO₄ solution contains 0.025 mol dm⁻³ SO₄⁻² ions.
moles of SO₄⁻² ions = 0.025 mol dm⁻³ × 2.00 dm³ = 0.05 mol

As Pb²⁺ and SO₄⁻² react in a 1 : 1 ratio, here, SO₄²⁻ (0.05 mol) will be consumed earlier than Pb²⁺ (0.0625 mol). The amount of SO₄⁻² will be limiting. The reason is that 0.05 mole of SO₄⁻² is less than 0.0625 mole of Pb²⁺. Since the Pb²⁺ ions are present in excess, only 0.05 mole of solid PbSO₄ will be formed. The mass of PbSO₄ formed can be calculated using the molar mass of PbSO₄ (303.3 g mol⁻¹):
blocks.answer: Mass of PbSO₄ = 0.05 mol × 303.3 g mol⁻¹ = 15.2 g

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed equation is not balanced: it has 2 Na on the left and 1 on the right. The balanced equation is Na₂SO₄(aq) + Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) → PbSO₄(s) + 2NaNO₃(aq). The 1 : 1 ratio of Pb²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ and the answer are not affected.
